questions.prompt: Sami spends his Saturdays taking old radios apart and putting them together again. Which intelligence does he show?
questions.explanation: "mechanical intelligence" is the one: it shows in somebody who likes building, repairing and finding out how an object works, which is exactly Sami's Saturday. "physical intelligence" would need energy and sport, "artistic intelligence" words or pictures, and "emotional intelligence" other people. A pair of hands on a radio proves none of those three.

questions.prompt: Which word names the wish to know and to find out about things you do not know yet?
questions.explanation: "curiosity" is the word: it names the wish itself, the thing that makes you open a book or ask one more question. "a brain" is the organ you think with, not a wish. "a gift" is a natural ability you already have, and "a prodigy" is a young person whose ability astonishes everybody.

questions.prompt: The questionnaire asks: "Can you express your feelings through pictures?" Which short answer is correct English?
questions.explanation: "Yes, I can." is correct: a short answer repeats the helper the question opens with, and this question opens with can. "Yes, I do." belongs to a question that begins with do, "Yes, I am." to one that begins with are you, and "Yes, I have." to one that begins with have you. Listen to the first word of the question, not to its meaning.

questions.prompt: A teacher wants to use the word prodigy in a school report. Which sentence can she write?

options.text: At eight he was a prodigy in mathematics.
He is prodigy at solving problems quickly.
Her prodigy appeared before she went to school.
She has a real prodigy for drawing.

questions.explanation: "At eight he was a prodigy in mathematics." is right: a prodigy is a young person, so you are one, and the age matters. "She has a real prodigy for drawing." and "Her prodigy appeared before she went to school." both treat the word as an ability, which is what a gift is. "He is prodigy at solving problems quickly." forgets that a countable noun naming a person needs its article.

questions.prompt: The acrostic poem of the lesson is built on the word STUDENT and has seven lines. How many times is the word student itself written inside a line?

options.text: once, at the beginning of the very first line
seven times, once in every line of the poem
twice, in the first and the last line
never: it is spelled by the first letters

questions.explanation: "never: it is spelled by the first letters" is right: that is the whole idea of an acrostic, where the word is read downwards, one letter per line, and never appears as a word. "once, at the beginning of the very first line" and "twice, in the first and the last line" would make the poem announce its own subject, and "seven times, once in every line of the poem" would leave nothing for the reader to discover.
